summary: For ages 11–12: extend place value as an unbounded ×10/÷10 structure (no largest or smallest place) and unify whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions onto ONE number line, where every number — however written — names a single point. Learners locate and order mixed forms by position relative to zero and to integer landmarks, recognising that a fraction and its decimal (e.g. 3/4 and 0.75) are the SAME point, and that on a standard (left-to-right) line ordering follows leftmost-is-smallest across all number types.
misconceptions: Thinking place value 'runs out' at a largest place (millions) or smallest place (thousandths)
Treating whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions as living on separate scales rather than one line
Placing negatives as if their magnitude sets their order (−3/4 to the left of −2)
Assuming a fraction and its decimal (3/4 and 0.75) are different points rather than the same point
Comparing mixed forms by surface features (digit count) rather than converting to a common form

activities.title: Many forms, one line
steps: Draw a single number line and place each of these numbers on it: −3/4, 0.6, −2, and 1.25. Then, on a separate zoomed-out view using an appropriate scale, mark a large integer such as 4,700,000, noting that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs both views.
For each number, say in words where it sits relative to zero and to the nearest whole-number landmarks (e.g. '1.25 is a quarter of the way from 1 to 2').
Place 3/4 and 0.75 separately, then check that both land on exactly the same point; write one sentence explaining why they must coincide.

Write all the numbers in order from smallest to largest, treating 3/4 and 0.75 as one point, and justify the order using position on the line, not the digits (−2 < −3/4 < 0.6 < 3/4 = 0.75 < 1.25 < 4,700,000).
activities.insight: Whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions all belong to one number line governed by a single ×10/÷10 structure; each names a single point and equivalent forms name the same point. On a standard (left-to-right) line, size is read as position (leftmost is smallest) across every type, even when very large and very small values must be shown at different scales.

activities.title: Zoom in — is there a smallest place?
steps: Take the segment from 0 to 1 and subdivide it into tenths; label 0.6 among them.
Zoom into a tenth (e.g. between 0.6 and 0.7) and subdivide into hundredths; place a value such as 0.65.
Zoom again into hundredths and mark thousandths; keep a note of which place column you are in at each step (tenths → hundredths → thousandths…).
Argue in writing whether this subdividing ever stops, and state what that means for a 'smallest place' in the place-value system.
Repeat the reasoning outward: explain why there is likewise no largest place as the ×10 structure grows.
activities.insight: The ×10/÷10 place-value structure continues without end in both directions — there is no smallest place and no largest place. Informally, between any two points more numbers can always be found, so any decimal or fraction has a location between landmarks.

activities.title: Value of a digit at any scale
steps: State the value of the 7 in 4,700,000 and the value of the 7 in 0.007.
For each, say which place column the 7 occupies and compute face value × place value.
Explain in one or two sentences why the same digit can represent vastly different amounts depending on its place.
Optional extension: explain to a partner (or in writing) why the place-value system has no largest and no smallest place.
activities.insight: A digit's value is its face value times its place value, and this scaling reasoning works for numbers of any size, large or small.

activities.title: Which is smaller, and why
steps: Place −3, 1/2 and 2.75 on one number line relative to zero and to each other.
Order them from smallest to largest.
Explain how you know −3 is the smallest, referring to its position rather than the size of the digit 3.
Name a number between 1/2 and 2.75, and then another number between those two, to show many values lie between any pair.
activities.insight: On a standard (left-to-right) number line, across all number types the leftmost position (furthest below zero) is smallest; a negative can be smaller than a small positive fraction even though its digit looks large. Informally, infinitely many numbers also lie between any two points.

checkQuestion: On one number line you have to place −3, 1/2 and 2.75. Where does each go relative to zero and to each other — and how do you know −3 is the smallest?
checkAnswer: −3 sits three to the LEFT of zero; 1/2 halfway between 0 and 1; 2.75 three-quarters of the way from 2 to 3. Ordered: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75. −3 is smallest because it is furthest left / below zero, regardless of the type of number.
